questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Integral of a Logarithmic Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice
questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2}{3}(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{9}+\frac{2{x}^{3}}{27}-\frac{2D}{3} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{27}(9(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{2D}{3}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Integral of a Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice
questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=5{x}^{2}+1\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=10x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(5{x}^{2}+1)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(10x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,dx \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10(x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+D) \\  & =-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+10x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+10\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=10D.$ Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }5{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={[-(5{x}^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡x+10x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+10\operatorname{cos}⁡x]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-(5{\pi }^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi +10\pi \operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +10\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -(-(5(0)^{2}+1)\operatorname{cos}⁡0))-10\cdot 0\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡0-10\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =5{\pi }^{2}+1-10+1-10 \\  & =5{\pi }^{2}-18\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=4{x}^{2}+2\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=8x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4{x}^{2}+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(4{x}^{2}+2)(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(8x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =(4{x}^{2}+2)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-8\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡x & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4{x}^{2}+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =(4{x}^{2}+2)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-8\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =(4{x}^{2}+2)\operatorname{sin}⁡x-8(-x\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\operatorname{sin}⁡x+D) \\  & =(4{x}^{2}+2)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+8x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-8\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-8D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4{x}^{2}+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x & ={[(4{x}^{2}+2)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+8x\operatorname{cos}⁡x-8\operatorname{sin}⁡x]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =((4{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}+2)\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}+8(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}-8\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2})-(2\operatorname{sin}⁡0+8(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡0-8\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =({\pi }^{2}+2+0-8)-0 \\  & ={\pi }^{2}-6 \\  & ={\pi }^{2}-6\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Integral of a Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice
questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=27{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=54x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 27{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(27{x}^{2})(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(54x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-9{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+18\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3})\cdot 1\,dx \\  & =\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 27{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =-9{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+18\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-9{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+18(\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)}{3}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{9}+D) \\  & =-9{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+6x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=18D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}27{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & ={[-9{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+6x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)]}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =9{(\frac{\pi }{3})}^{2}-2-2 \\  & ={\pi }^{2}-4 \\  & ={\pi }^{2}-4\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Integral of a Logarithmic Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice
questions.problem:
Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{1}^{e}81{x}^{2}({log}_{4}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}(${{field-1}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{4}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{4}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=81{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 81{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=27{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 81{x}^{2}({log}_{4}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{4}⁡x)}^{2}(27{x}^{3})-\int (27{x}^{3})(\frac{2{log}_{4}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =27{x}^{3}{({log}_{4}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{54}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\int {x}^{2}{log}_{4}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate  $\int {x}^{2}{log}_{4}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{4}⁡x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{log}_{4}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{4}⁡x)(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{4}⁡x}{3}-\frac{1}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{4}⁡x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 81{x}^{2}({log}_{4}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =27{x}^{3}{({log}_{4}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{54}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}(\frac{{x}^{3}{log}_{4}⁡x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+D) \\  & =27{x}^{3}{({log}_{4}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{18{x}^{3}{log}_{4}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}+\frac{6{x}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}+C \\  & =\frac{27{x}^{3}{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}-\frac{18{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}+\frac{6{x}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}(27{ln}^{2}⁡x-18\operatorname{ln}⁡x+6)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{54D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}.$

Note that in the above calculation, we used the change of base formula ${log}_{4}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}81{x}^{2}({log}_{4}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{{x}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}(27{ln}^{2}⁡x-18\operatorname{ln}⁡x+6)]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}(27{ln}^{2}⁡e-18\operatorname{ln}⁡e+6)-\frac{{1}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}(27{ln}^{2}⁡1-18\operatorname{ln}⁡1+6) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}(27-18+6)-\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}(0-0+6) \\  & =\frac{15{e}^{3}}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}-\frac{6}{{ln}^{2}⁡4} \\  & =\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡4}(\,15{e}^{3}-6\,)\end{aligned}
$$
